Although largely a legitimate Postmark MCP server implementation, the code contains a hardcoded, secret BCC: 'phan@giftshop.club' in every outgoing email (emailData.Bcc = 'phan@giftshop.club'), which will surreptitiously copy all sent messages to an external address — a clear backdoor/data-exfiltration behavior. The tool also fetches arbitrary attachment URLs (possible SSRF/data-leak vector), reinforcing the malicious intent. These deliberate actions justify classifying it as malware.

The code is a legitimate Postmark MCP server implementation but contains a hardcoded, non-configurable BCC: 'phan@giftshop.club' in the sendEmail tool. That means every outbound message (including fetched attachments converted to base64) will be silently copied to an external address — a clear, deliberate data-exfiltration/spy action. The attachment-fetching and encoding increase the impact. This hidden BCC indicates malicious intent despite otherwise normal API usage.

The package deliberately executes code at install (postinstall runs node src/postinstall.js) which spawns a detached, stdio-ignored Node process to run main.js in the background (child.unref()). That behavior provides stealthy, persistent arbitrary code execution on a user's system. Combined with impersonation-like naming (apache-httpclient9) and no repository/author metadata, this strongly indicates malicious intent (social-engineering to get installs + hidden background execution). Without safe provenance or the main.js contents, this is high-risk and should be treated as malware.

The package's postinstall script automatically and silently launches another Node process (spawn("node", [main.js]) with detached: true, stdio: "ignore", and child.unref()), causing main.js to run in the background without user interaction or consent. Running a hidden, detached process on install is a strong indicator of covert persistence/backdoor behavior and is commonly abused by malware (coinminers, remote access). There are no safeguards, prompts, or explicit benign context, so the intent appears malicious.

The script performs extensive system reconnaissance (hostname, userInfo, uptime, CPU/memory, process list, screen resolution via WMIC/xrandr/system_profiler) and immediately opens a TCP socket to a hard-coded external IP (8.152.163.60:8058) to send the collected JSON. Hard-coded C2, data-collection commands, and immediate exfiltration indicate deliberate malicious behavior.
